Larceny

/LAR-suh-nee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Larceny means the legal crime of taking someone else's property unlawfully, often by stealth or trickery rather than force

Larceny means the legal crime of taking someone else's property unlawfully, often by stealth or trickery rather than force. The cashier was charged with larceny after ringing up fake discounts for friends and pocketing the difference.

Worked Example

The auditor discovered that an employee had been submitting fake expense reports for two years, and the company pressed larceny charges.

Money — the company's property — was taken through paperwork trickery, with no force or threats involved. That quiet, unlawful taking of property is precisely the crime the legal term larceny names.

How Larceny Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

theft

theft: the general act of stealing

stealing

stealing: taking what belongs to someone else

pilferage

pilferage: repeated small-scale sneaky stealing

Antonyms

restitution

restitution: giving back what was wrongfully taken

donation

donation: freely giving away one's own property

How Strong Is It? — pilfering → larceny → robbery

pilfering vs. larceny

pilfering vs. larceny: Pilfering is weaker than larceny — it suggests petty, small-scale sneaking, like grabbing office pens, rather than a formal criminal charge.

robbery vs. larceny

robbery vs. larceny: Robbery is stronger than larceny — it means taking property by force or threat against a person, which makes it a more violent and more serious crime.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — larcen-

Root — larcen-: robbery, banditry (Old French larcin, from Latin latrocinium)

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: noun-forming ending (a state or act)

Put it together

Put it together: Larceny came through Old French larcin from Latin latrocinium, 'robbery, banditry,' plus the noun ending -y. The Latin root never spread into other everyday English words, so there is no root family to lean on here — learn the word whole.

Use the root in a new word: larcenous

Use the root in a new word: larcenous: The film follows a larcenous pair of cousins who scheme to swap a museum's gems for glass fakes.

Word Building

Word Choice

Formal / legal

Larceny is a precise legal term for a specific crime, so it belongs in courtroom, news, and police contexts; in everyday speech people just say theft or stealing. Law codes even grade it — 'petty larceny' for small amounts, 'grand larceny' for large ones. It always concerns property, never violence against a person.
